Pronounce it as: VY-vah VOH-chay

It rhymes roughly with "I-va OH-shay." The phrase comes from Latin, so the pronunciation follows Latin rules, not English ones.

"Viva voce" is a Latin phrase. Breaking it down word by word:

  • Viva means "living" or "alive"
  • Voce means "voice"

So, put together, it literally means "with the living voice." In plain English, this simply means: spoken aloud, by a real human voice, in real time.

The idea behind the phrase is the contrast between something written down (fixed, static, silent on a page) and something spoken out loud (alive, immediate, in the moment).
The Core Meaning in Everyday Use

When someone says something is done "viva voce," they mean it is done orally — by speaking — rather than in writing. That's the heart of it. If you're ever unsure, just replace "viva voce" in a sentence with the word "oral" or "spoken" and the meaning will almost always hold perfectly.
Where You'll Most Commonly Encounter It

1. In Academia (The Most Common Use)

This is where you'll encounter "viva voce" most often. In universities — especially in the UK, Ireland, Australia, India, and other countries that follow the British academic tradition — a viva voce is a formal oral examination.

It is often shortened simply to "a viva." You'll frequently hear students say, "I have my viva next week," and it means exactly the same thing.

How it works:

A student who has written a large piece of academic work — most commonly a PhD thesis (a book-length research dissertation) or sometimes a Master's dissertation — must sit in front of a panel of expert examiners and defend their work out loud. The examiners ask probing questions, and the student must answer them verbally, on the spot, demonstrating that:

  • They truly understand their own research deeply.
  • They can explain and justify every decision, argument, and conclusion they made in their written work.
  • They have genuine expertise in their subject area.
  • The work is authentically their own.

This is why the oral element is so important — a written exam alone can't easily verify these things the same way a live conversation can. The "living voice" reveals knowledge, understanding, and authenticity in a way that ink on paper cannot.

A simple example to picture it:

Imagine you spent five years writing a 90,000-word research thesis on climate change. The viva voce is the moment you sit in a room with two senior professors and they ask you, face to face: "Why did you choose this methodology? What are the weaknesses of your argument on page 147? How does your work fit into the existing research landscape?" You must answer confidently and knowledgeably. It can last anywhere from one hour to several hours.

2. In Law and Formal Proceedings

In legal contexts, "viva voce evidence" means testimony given out loud in court, as opposed to written statements submitted on paper. When a witness stands in the witness box and speaks their testimony directly to the court, that is viva voce evidence. Legal systems often place high value on this because it allows cross-examination, lets the judge and jury observe the witness in real time, and holds the speaker directly accountable for what they say.

3. In Voting (Historical Use)

Historically, "viva voce voting" referred to a method of casting votes by calling them out verbally in a public assembly, rather than by secret written ballot. Voters would literally say their choice aloud. This method is now largely obsolete in most democratic systems because it lacked secrecy and could expose voters to pressure or intimidation.

In everyday speech, particularly among students and academics, the phrase is almost always shortened to just "viva." You will rarely hear someone say the full "viva voce" in casual conversation. Both forms are correct; "viva voce" is more formal and precise, while "viva" is the practical, everyday shorthand.
Why Use a Latin Phrase at All?

You might wonder — why not just say "oral exam"? The answer lies in history. Latin was the universal language of scholarship, law, and the church in medieval and early modern Europe. Universities were founded during this era, and their traditions, ceremonies, and technical vocabulary were built in Latin. Many of these Latin terms stuck around and became embedded in academic and legal culture. "Viva voce" is one of them — it carries centuries of tradition with it, and it has a precise, unambiguous meaning that professionals in those fields continue to find useful.

One Sentence to Remember It Forever

"Viva voce" means anything done with the spoken, living voice — most famously, the oral examination where a student defends their thesis in person before expert examiners.

Once you know that "voce" gives us the English word "vocal," and "viva" connects to words like "vivid" and "vivacious" (all suggesting life and energy), the phrase becomes almost self-explanatory: a living, vocal, in-person exchange.
